The passage begins by asserting that Byzantine history after 1370 became "a mere piece of local history," no longer forming "an important thread in the history of Christendom" [PDF p. 358]. The author argues that Murad’s potential conquest of Constantinople in 1370 would not have significantly altered European events, as the empire ceased to function as "bulwark of Christendom" after losing its protective role. The Paleologi’s "base subservience to the Turk" prolonged the empire’s existence despite its original purpose having disappeared [PDF p. 358].  

Middle sections detail Manuel II’s reign amid Ottoman civil wars. In 1402, Timur’s invasion defeated Sultan Bayezid, creating opportunities for Manuel. The author explains how Manuel capitalized on Ottoman infighting, recovering territories including Constantinople, Thessalonica, and the Peloponnesus [PDF p. 360-361]. Despite Ottoman reunification under Mohammed, Manuel maintained control through alliances until 1421 [PDF p. 361]. However, the author emphasizes that European powers failed to exploit Ottoman weakness, noting "Europe had an unparalleled opportunity... but it was not taken" [PDF p. 362].  

The ending describes Murad II’s siege of Constantinople [PDF p. 363]. Though cannons and Janissaries attacked, the city repelled assaults [PDF p. 364]. Manuel died in 1422, succeeded by John VI, whose reign featured Ottoman annexation of Thessalonica [PDF p. 366-367]. The author attributes the empire’s final decline to its reduced state: Constantinople’s population dwindled, Italian merchants dominated commerce, and the emperor’s court shrank to "eight attendants" [PDF p. 366]. The passage concludes that John VI’s attempts to gain Western support through religious conformity yielded minimal aid [PDF p. 367], leaving the empire in "unredeemed gloom" [PDF p. 365].
